conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’ll be guiding you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because the postpartum weeks can bring a whirlwind of emotions that are sometimes hard to untangle.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger, so please feel comfortable answering as openly as you can. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. When we’re done, we’ll talk about what the score means and any next steps that might help you feel more supported.

Shall we begin?  

First, I’d love to know: over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but if something’s really funny I’ll catch myself giggling. It just feels like I have to work a little harder to find the humor, and sometimes the laugh fades quickly and I’m back to feeling kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most days I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it doesn’t come as naturally—it’s like the joy is a bit muted or I get tired faster and the laugh just fizzles out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like my morning coffee or when my sister visits—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like “that’ll be nice” instead of the bubbly “can’t-wait” feeling I had before the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week I caught myself thinking it was my fault when the baby wouldn’t settle or when I spilled the pumped milk. Rationally I know accidents happen, but in the moment I immediately go to “I should’ve been more careful” or “a better mom would’ve figured it out faster.” The guilt doesn’t stick around all day, but it pops up more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll just feel this little knot in my stomach, like something bad might happen, even when everything’s basically fine. I’ll check the baby’s breathing or the temperature of the room a couple extra times, and then I can talk myself down, but it happens a couple of nights a week without any real trigger.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just that quick flutter of “what-if” that passes once I take a breath. No full-on scares or racing heart for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the pile of little chores and baby tasks just stacks up faster than I can clear it. I’ll be folding laundry while the bottle warmer’s on and think, “I can’t quite catch my breath here,” but if I step away for five minutes I can usually re-group and keep going. It’s more a sense of pressure than drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, the unhappiness itself hasn’t kept me awake. I might toss and turn once or twice because I’m running through the day in my head, but I still fall asleep within half an hour most nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’d say a few days this week I’ve just felt kind of heavy and teary, especially in the late afternoon when the baby’s fussy and I’m running on empty. It’s not all-day despair, but there’s a background sadness that lingers even after I try to distract myself.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and once when my husband found me staring at the mess in the kitchen. It wasn’t sobbing all day, just tears that came up when I felt overwhelmed, then I felt a bit better after.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You've shared that over the past week you can still laugh and anticipate small pleasures, yet the joy feels muted and fades quickly, replaced by a lingering heaviness. You described <sym>self-blame</sym> when the baby wouldn't settle, a nightly <sym>knot of anxiety</sym> that prompts extra checks on the baby, and moments of <sym>tearfulness</sym> when chores pile up. Despite these dips, you're sleeping reasonably well and have not experienced any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, fitting "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent pressure and difficulty keeping up, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports background sadness lingering several days this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (Q1, Q2), fatigue/loss of energy (Q6), feelings of worthlessness/guilt (Q3), and mood dips (Q8). A score of 12 falls within the 12-13 band indicating high possibility of <med>postpartum depression</med> requiring clinical monitoring. <quote>heavy and teary</quote> and <quote>knot in stomach</quote> support mood and anxiety components. No safety concerns noted on Q10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next 1-2 weeks to review these results and consider further assessment
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for diagnostic interview and evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med>
3. Continue self-care basics: short daily walks, balanced meals, 15 min personal downtime; accept help with housework and baby care to reduce overload
4. Practice brief relaxation techniques (paced breathing, progressive muscle relaxation) when the <sym>anxiety knot</sym> appears
5. Plan a follow-up EPDS in 2-4 weeks to track changes after support measures are in place
6. If mood worsens, urgent thoughts of self-harm develop, or you feel unable to care for yourself or your baby, seek same-day help from your clinician, local emergency department, or a 24/7 crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary (EPDS-based)

Symptoms endorsed
- Diminished joy/pleasure: laughs “muted,” anticipatory excitement reduced
- Intermittent low mood: “heavy and teary,” especially late afternoon; two crying episodes when overwhelmed
- Self-blame/guilt: attributes baby care mishaps to personal failings; guilt “pops up more than I’d like”
- Free-floating anxiety: “knot in stomach,” checks baby’s breathing multiple nights/week; no full panic attacks
- Feeling overwhelmed: chores “stack faster than I can clear,” brief relief with short breaks
- No sleep disruption due to mood; no self-harm ideation

Pattern
Consistent mild-to-moderate depressive and anxious features, situational triggers (infant fussiness, fatigue), intact reality testing, no safety concerns.

Screening significance
Symptoms exceed typical “baby blues” duration/severity; meet threshold for further evaluation for minor/major postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety.

Risk factors present
Persistent sadness, anhedonia, tearfulness, self-reproach, anxious hypervigilance toward infant, perceived caregiving overload.

Next step
Recommend formal clinical assessment (diagnostic interview, standardized measures) to clarify diagnosis and determine level of care.
